name: Cath Carroll
label: Factory Records
lede: A Manchester fanzine editor turned NME writer turned Factory singer spent two years and four studios on one album, recorded in Sheffield, São Paulo, London and Chicago, then moved to Chicago for good.

eras.title: City Fun and the Gay Animals
eras.text: Born in Chipping Sodbury in 1960 and raised in Swansea, Ipswich and Manchester, Cath Carroll came up through Manchester post-punk as a player and a writer at once. She and Liz Naylor ran a fanzine that Factory read closely and a band whose name changed once.

years.src: Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: Carroll plays guitar in Property Of… with an ex-Warsaw drummer
years.p: Her first band includes Tony Tabac, who had drummed in Warsaw before it became [[Joy Division|9a58fda3-f4ed-4080-a3a5-f457aac9fcdd]].

years.src: Scream City · Chicago Reader · Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: Carroll and Liz Naylor start Glass Animals, soon Gay Animals
years.p: Pip from [[The Distractions|6590cdda-6eb7-44d5-b17e-d94a0497e885]] drums. By 1980 the name is Gay Animals, and the pair have taken over the City Fun fanzine.
years.xp:
City Fun started as a collective led by Andy Zero; Carroll and Naylor kept turning up to editorial meetings until it was theirs. "Every fortnight we'd have these hideously grueling all night layout sessions," Carroll told Scream City.

The Chicago Reader says Factory were fans of the zine, and that the two had first memberships at the Haçienda. Carroll later learned [[Tony Wilson|124a6f5d-b2e0-4a75-95ad-db4c38063e02]] had been hurt by what they wrote: "Everything we'd written, we'd written affectionately."

years.src: Wikipedia: Cath Carroll · LTM: Cath Carroll
years.h: London, NME and a pen name: Myrna Minkoff
years.p: Gay Animals end when Carroll moves to London. She writes for NME and City Limits as Myrna Minkoff and starts a new band, Miaow.

eras.title: Miaow on C86
eras.text: Miaow played the jangly guitar pop the NME was busy naming, and Carroll was one of the writers doing the naming. A demo got them to Factory, and two singles followed.

years.src: Wikipedia: Miaow · LTM: Cath Carroll
years.h: Miaow's first single, "Belle Vue", on Venus
years.p: Carroll sings and plays guitar with Steve Maguire, Ron Caine and Chris Fenner. "Fate" is the B-side.

years.src: Wikipedia: Miaow · Wikipedia: Cath Carroll · Scream City
years.h: "Sport Most Royal" lands on NME's C86 tape
years.p: Miaow share the cassette with [[Primal Scream|55704c38-224f-4b75-b29f-d43653f8bc9a]] and [[The Wedding Present|707622da-475f-48e1-905d-248718df6521]], and record their first Peel session in June.

years.src: Wikipedia: Miaow · Cerysmatic Factory: Cath Carroll · LTM: Cath Carroll
years.h: Tony Wilson hears a demo and Factory issues "When It All Comes Down"
years.p: FAC 179 reaches No. 5 on the indie chart. A second Peel session went down in January.

years.src: Wikipedia: Miaow · Cerysmatic Factory: Cath Carroll
years.h: "Break the Code", FAC 189, gets to No. 18
years.p: Miaow's second Factory single. The band also tour the UK supporting [[The Woodentops|90ae37a5-a693-4f81-893a-ca07ed365bdf]].

eras.title: Samba, Sheffield and Chicago
eras.text: Miaow broke up before they made an album, and Factory backed Carroll alone. The record took two years and four cities, and by the time it came out she was living in Chicago with a former Big Black guitarist.

years.src: LTM: Cath Carroll · Wikipedia: Miaow
years.h: Miaow end with their album, Priceless Innuendo, unfinished
years.p: The Factory demo survives; LTM's When It All Comes Down compilation collects the band in 2003.

years.src: Wikipedia: England Made Me · Scream City · LTM: Cath Carroll
years.h: Carroll starts England Made Me at FON in Sheffield
years.p: She works with [[Sim Lister|92e18803-eccb-4fc3-aa6f-5f21d47ea11e]] and Marc Brydon, later of [[Moloko|2f94016a-3880-4d8c-9af9-0e197ee77189]], then takes the tapes to Cardan Studios in São Paulo, Blackwing in London and Chicago Recording Company.
years.xp:
The batucada came from the London School of Samba. "I wanted to do something with those rhythms," Carroll said, and she heard in them something close to rockabilly and cajun.

In Chicago [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]] produced "Train You're On", and Big Black's [[Santiago Durango|00aa2c29-22a9-4e55-a01b-e51896a379a3]] played. "It wasn't a deliberate blending, but more an assembly of things I liked," she told Scream City.

years.src: Wikipedia: Cath Carroll · Chicago Reader · Scream City
years.h: Carroll moves to Chicago for Santiago Durango
years.p: She met the ex-[[Big Black|9463868f-edc8-427e-ac07-ea89698e5f15]] guitarist on Big Black's British tour; he was at law school. In Chicago she works with house producer Vince Lawrence.
years.xp: "After years of suspicion, I had finally started to think of the USA as somewhere I'd like to live," she told Scream City. The Chicago Reader put it more simply: she came for love. Carroll and Durango married.

years.src: Wikipedia: England Made Me · Cerysmatic Factory: Cath Carroll
years.h: "Beast", FAC 255, is the first single from the album
years.p: Factory puts it out a year before the LP.

years.src: Discogs: Moves Like You · Wikipedia: England Made Me
years.h: "Moves Like You", FAC 307, with a Douglas Brothers sleeve
years.p: The 12-inch backs it with "Too Good to Live" and an "Angel" remix. Design by Two, photography by the Douglas Brothers.

years.cap: Cath Carroll at a dressing-room door, c. 1991
years.src: Q Magazine · Wikipedia: England Made Me
years.h: England Made Me is out, two years after it started
years.p: FACT 210, named after the Graham Greene novel. The title track is her goodbye to Thatcher's England, what she called her Billy Bragg number.
years.xp:
Q reported that Wilson bankrolled the two-year project, a mix of samba, art-rock and dance. Carroll, 30, told the magazine she didn't like asserting herself and thought it vulgar to say "I" too much.

Reviews were mixed, with praise for the atmosphere and doubts about her languid delivery. AllMusic later said it prefigured the female-fronted dance pop to come.

years.src: Scream City · LTM: Cath Carroll
years.h: Factory goes under, and Wilson tells a hot dog story
years.p: LTM says the album's budget was cited as one factor in the collapse. Wilson's version, as Carroll told it in 2006: she took Factory's money to America to start a hot dog stand.
years.xp:
"He keeps, even now, telling this story about how we owe him £5K for a magazine he backed," Carroll told Scream City. By her account it was £50, and they hoped it was a grant.

The other half of the story is the hot dog stand, which she says never happened.

eras.title: Teenbeat, Lilypad and two books
eras.text: In Chicago Carroll kept making records on small labels, wrote about other people's, and turned into a song title herself.

years.src: Wikipedia: Perfect Teeth · Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: Unrest name a song "Cath Carroll"
years.p: [[Mark Robinson|fc1a1e50-b6f7-431f-834b-d1441e54dcb7]]'s band put it second on Perfect Teeth, out on 4AD, and a Cath Carroll EP follows on TeenBeat.

years.src: LTM: Cath Carroll · Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: True Crime Motel on TeenBeat
years.p: After the singles "My Cold Heart" and "Bad Star", an album LTM calls noir, sung in an understated voice.

years.src: LTM: Cath Carroll · Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: A self-titled album on Lilypad
years.p: LTM hears Astrud Gilberto and [[Roxy Music|331ce348-1b08-40b9-8ed7-0763b92bd003]] in it. It is reissued in 2010 as Glommer.

years.src: Wikipedia: Cath Carroll · Wikipedia: England Made Me
years.h: LTM puts out The Gondoliers of Ghost Lake
years.p: The same year LTM reissues England Made Me with four bonus tracks.

years.src: Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: Carroll writes a book on Fleetwood Mac's Rumours
years.p: Never Break the Chain comes out on Chicago Review Press, three years after her critical discography of [[Tom Waits|c3aeb863-7b26-4388-94e8-5a240f2be21b]].

years.src: Wikipedia: Cath Carroll
years.h: Guest vocals for Trembling Blue Stars and the Hit Parade
years.p: She sings on [[Trembling Blue Stars|59a2e877-0571-40c3-a405-2e52b170fa2c]]' Fast Trains and Telegraph Wires, and in 2014 on three songs of [[The Hit Parade|97205704-b75d-4287-b1d4-ce4ead1367c1]]'s Cornish Pop Songs.
